Fig. 1 | Mining bacterial genomes for new NPs. a | In bacterial genomes, 
biosynthetic genes are usually located side by side in one locus, named a 
biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC). BGC representation shown resembles the 
erythromycin BGC. A BGC is typically composed of biosynthetic core genes 
(dark blue) that encode the biosynthetic machinery assembling the natural 
product (NP) scaffold, and additional biosynthetic genes (dark pink) such as 
methyltransferases or glycosyltransferases that further modify the scaffold or 
synthesize precursors. In addition, self-resistance genes (green, for antibiotics), 
regulatory elements (pale pink) and hypothetical genes (pale blue) are usually 
co-localized. Proximity of these genes allows their efficient detection through

figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 2 | Experimental strategies to functionally link BGCs with their respective NPs. Methods applied in discovery 
processes of the displayed example compounds isolated from non-classical, talented bacterial natural product (NP) 
producers (bioactivities listed after compound name): biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) inactivation, a classical 
strategy to yield producing and non-producing strains (panel a); expression of inactive (silent) BGCs can be induced 
by overexpression of transcription factors (panel b), native promoter exchange to an inducible promoter (panel c), 
BGC expression in a heterologous host (panel d), addition of BGC activators (panel e) or quorum-sensing manipulation 
(panel f); all strategies aim for a comparison of metabolic profiles or phenotypes to correlate the presence of a BGC 
with a produced NP (panel g); and comparison can be further informed by substructure prediction in vitro to guide 
NP isolation and structure elucidation (panel h).

figure_candidates.label: Figure 3
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 3 | Examples of ecology-guided approaches and compounds discovered by them. Pederin-type natural products 
(NPs) have been isolated from various symbiotic hosts, including psyllids, marine sponges, beetles and lichen (part a). 
Other NPs have only been isolated from unique ecological niches such as oligotrophic leaf surfaces (part b) or marine 
sediments (part c). Bioactive NPs might also play an important role in insect–microorganism interactions, mediating, 
for example, defensive symbioses of beewolf digger wasps that harbour antibiotic-producing Streptomyces spp. 
in their antennae (part d) or protection of insect eggs (part e). Complex interactions observed for bacterial members  
of microbiomes from, for example, the human nose have also proven a rich source for new antibiotics (part f). Another 
important ecology-guided NP discovery approach lies in exploiting predation and protection against being consumed; 
examples include corallopyronin that originates in myxobacterial predation (part g) or termite fungal gardens that 
protect against microbial predators (part h). The bioactivities are listed after the compound name.
